You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
" *

Adds all the elements of the given arrays into a new array.

*

The new array contains all of the element of array1 followed * by all of the elements array2. When an array is returned, it is always * a new array.

* * 
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(null, null)     = null
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(array1, null)   = cloned copy of array1
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(null, array2)   = cloned copy of array2
     * ArrayUtils.addAll([], [])         = []
     * ArrayUtils.addAll([null], [null]) = [null, null]
     * ArrayUtils.addAll(["a", "b", "c"], ["1", "2", "3"]) = ["a", "b", "c", "1", "2", "3"]
     *
* * @param array1 the first array whose elements are added to the new array, may be null * @param array2 the second array whose elements are added to the new array, may be null * @return The new array, null if both arrays are null. * The type of the new array is the type of the first array, * unless the first array is null, in which case the type is the same as the second array. * @since 2.1 "

Diagnosis:
The test case `testJira567()` verifies the behavior of the method `ArrayUtils.addAll(T[] array1, T... array2)` when adding elements from two arrays of possibly different types. The test first confirms that combining two arrays of the same supertype (Number[]) but different subtype elements (Integer and Long) works fine. Then it verifies that attempting to add arrays of incompatible types (Integer[] and Long[]) throws an IllegalArgumentException.

The method `ArrayUtils.addAll(T[] array1, T... array2)` retrieves the component type of the first array and creates a new array of that type large enough to hold elements from both input arrays. It copies the elements of the first array to the new array and then copies elements of the second array using `System.arraycopy`.

The observed failure is an ArrayStoreException at `System.arraycopy` when trying to mix incompatible types `Integer[]` and `Long[]`. This is because `System.arraycopy` will throw ArrayStoreException if elements from the source array cannot be stored in the destination array's component type. The current code does not perform a check to ensure that elements in `array2` can be stored in the new array type (the component type of `array1`). Instead, it blindly copies the arrays.

The test expects an IllegalArgumentException to be thrown when the types are incompatible, but the current code lets the underlying JVM throw ArrayStoreException, which is less informative and not compliant with the expected behavior.

Hence, the bug is that `ArrayUtils.addAll` does not validate the type compatibility of the elements of `array2` against the component type of `array1` before arraycopy, resulting in ArrayStoreException instead of a clear IllegalArgumentException.

The recent bug reports do not provide relevant information related to this type compatibility or validation issue. They mainly address generic utilities and validation methods unrelated to this specific array type problem.

In summary, the root cause is the lack of explicit type compatibility check for the second array's elements in `ArrayUtils.addAll(T[], T...)`.

Suggested fix approach is to add a check before copying `array2` to ensure all its elements can be cast to the type of `array1`'s component type and throw IllegalArgumentException if not.

The method to fix is therefore `ArrayUtils.addAll(T[] array1, T... array2)`.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
